utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very short administrative matter, Your Honour. There is forthcoming two witnesses of an expert character, Terzic and Popov by surname, and I think that there may be outstanding applications and orders to be made in respect of them. I'm not sure about the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have made an order which I think you should get. I signed it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For Terzic. And what's the other one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Popov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: An order will be made in respect of the other witness by Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That will enable us to deal with them in a timely way. More generally, there was a -- I think an order, I haven't dug it up yet - again, my mistake - that we should be having 50 witnesses pretty well notified at a time. We've got the accused's list of witnesses until the Christmas break, and there may be some spill-over, I dare say, of the last couple of witnesses into the New Year, but our invitations to be provided with a list of witnesses who are going to come after the Christmas break has so far not been answered. Now, if we are to prepare these witnesses we really do need advance notice. We simply can't prepare witnesses without advance notice. And of course as the Chamber will have, I dare say, forecast when looking at the 65 ter summaries initially and will have discovered on seeing the evidence given by witnesses foreshadowed only by a four- or five-line 65 ter summary, preparation is very difficult without the sort of detail that would be provided by a Prosecution to a Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How many witnesses are on the accused's list to December?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only about another six, I think. Terzic, Popov --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In any event, the accused will have to present another list before the end of this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Another list of witnesses that will take us through January and February and March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And we'll make an order to that effect shortly. Mr. Milosevic, call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I call the next witness, I just have a motion, a submission; namely, yesterday Mr. Primakov mentioned his book titled Eight Months Plus, and part of the examination, especially cross-examination, had to do with his conversation with Chirac pertaining his visit to Belgrade and there also his conversations with Gore, with Kofi Annan in that book. I'm not going to go into the details of those conversations, however, this is a very useful material. Therefore, I was going to ask you to admit that book into evidence as well, this book of Mr. Primakov that he mentioned yesterday. If you wish, if you accept this, I will prepare it and submit it to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Submit it to us, and we'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I call witness Vukasin Jokanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm reminded that of course it's only the parts of the book that are relevant that were adverted to that we would consider admitting, so that you should identify those parts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And of course the obvious point is that I wasn't alerted to it and may have had several questions to ask arising out of it, but perhaps I could see the book when it is admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may begin, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Jokanovic.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us your full name and last name.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Vukasin Jokanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were born and you lived for a long time in Kosovo and Metohija. You were schooled there up until the university level. Please tell us briefly something about your biography.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I spent most of my life in Kosovo. I lived and worked there for a long time. I completed my elementary and secondary school in Kosovo, and law school in Macedonia in Skopje. After completing the law school I worked in Gnjilane for about 14 hours. Out of that time I spent eight years as president of the municipality of Gnjilane. I had two terms of four years, then I was a member of the Council of Kosovo and a commission on the -- legislative commission of the province in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, please slow down a little bit. And let us just clarify: The municipality of Gnjilane is in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: After my term, four-year term, as a member of the Presidency of Kosovo, I was also a member of -- of another organ within the province of Kosovo, and then I became a deputy in the Assembly of Kosovo. I served two terms there, two one-year terms because, in accordance with our then system, the terms lasted one year and anybody could be elected for two terms. In late 1989, I went to work in Belgrade. I was vice-president of the Assembly of Serbia and also a delegate in the Assembly of Serbia. Then I was a federal delegate and president of the Commission for Justice and Administration. I was a minister in the government, and my last post was the federal prosecutor of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I retired two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jokanovic. At the time when the Assembly of Kosovo debated and decided on the amendments of the constitution of Serbia in 1989, you were president of the Assembly of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was president of the Assembly during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is a very important issue, and I want us to go into that. I wanted to start off with that question, but since we need to watch a tape, I was told by the registry that it would be better to put it off for a bit later. So we will now turn to other issues and then come back to this issue later. Mr. Jokanovic, Kosovo and Metohija is an ethnically mixed territory, or at least it used to be. What was the ethnic composition in the organs in which you worked and generally in various other organs and organisations?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Ethnic composition in organs and organisations depended on the ethnic composition of the population. That was one of the key positions in the policy that was conducted in Kosovo at the time, so that in all posts starting at the municipal level up until the level of the province, and also at the republic level and federal level, depended on the ethnic composition of the population. This is how it was in the organs, social organs and socio-political organs and in the economy. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you were president of the Assembly in 1989, do you remember who were main political figures in Kosovo and Metohija as well as do you remember who were main political figures from Kosovo and Metohija in Serbia and at the federation level?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly I remember. I was president of the Assembly. My vice-president was an Albanian. The general secretary was an Albanian. The Assembly had three Chambers. Each Chamber had its president, out of which two were Albanians and one Montenegrin. President of the Kosovo Presidency, which was the highest collective organ, was also led by an Albanian. President of the Province Committee was also an Albanian. President of the Socialist Alliance, which was the largest social organisation, was also an Albanian. President of the union was a Serb, and president of the youth organisation was also an Albanian. And at the level of the federation, the most responsible posts were generally held by Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jokanovic. Please tell me, when was the first time that you were faced with the phenomenon of Albanian separatism in Kosovo? Or let me rephrase it: With the phenomenon of the organised Albanian separatism in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The first time I was faced with the organised expression of Albanian separatism and nationalism was in 1968. That year, in several cities in Kosovo, demonstrations were organised. They were also organised in Gnjilane, which is where I worked and lived. These demonstrations were held on the 27th of November, on the eve of the state holiday of Albania, which is on the 28th of November. That was my first encounter with the organised activities, with demonstrations held in the streets, with people carrying well-known slogans.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us in more detail what those demonstrations were like. What was their objective, and what was their scope?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The main objective of the demonstrations could be seen from the slogans which were shouted. The slogans were "Kosovo Republic," and "Unification." These slogans dominated, and there were other slogans as well. The demonstrations I witnessed myself in Gnjilane mostly included younger people in the streets. And later on, through our political work, we learned who the organisers were, whom we criticised. These people were in the vicinity of the demonstrators. And there were also a lot of people standing there just out of curiosity and watching it. The demonstrations in Gnjilane started in front of the secondary school centre, then they passed through the entire city and went to the bus station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, I have to interrupt you to save time. You don't have to give us very detailed description. Please tell us, what were the main slogans?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The main slogans were "Kosovo Republic" and "Unification."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, this information that I have, that the demonstrations were very severe in Gnjilane, Urosevac, and so on? So in Kosovo, but the demonstrations were also held in Western Macedonia, especially in Tetovo.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The most -- the most important demonstrations were held there in Gnjilane and so on, and also in Western Macedonia, in Tetovo, where the police organs of the Republic of Macedonia acted very severely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, in 1968, when these demonstrations were held, how did official organs qualify the demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: In the municipality where I worked and at the province level, the official organs qualified these demonstrations as being against the constitutional system, against the equality of nations and nationalities, against brotherhood and unity, as we used to say then, and it was also qualified that those demonstrations were aimed at destroying our constitutional systems, the system of self-management, and all other values of our then system, including the policies of Comrade Tito as we used to call him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These events in 1968, were they covered in the media?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Very briefly. There was an attempt to cover that up. Those were the times and the circumstances. It was believed that something like that could not happen in the socialist Yugoslavia when Tito was at the zenith of his power and authority. So there was an attempt to cover this up and it was basically not covered in the press. However, throughout the municipality where I worked and I was politically active, there were various meetings organised. So together with Albanians, I went out in the field to explain the essence of those demonstrations and to criticise them verbally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So the media tried to cover up those events. Do you know, was the army used on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The army was not used in Gnjilane. However, it was used in Pristina and Urosevac, as far as I know. And I know that because in the following days I travelled to Pristina and I came back through Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We don't need to go into detail. So your answer is yes, the army was used.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to a lesser extent than in other demonstrations that followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, if you could tell us what you were, by profession, in 1968.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1968, I was assistant to the director of the medical centre in Gnjilane, in charge of legal and economic issues at the medical centre which comprised hospital, health centre, pharmacy, and other medical services institutions. I was also politically active. I was also a member of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, you mentioned the position of President Tito. How did the Albanians view President Tito?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Comrade Tito, as we called him, visited Kosovo on a number of occasions. He was always greeted by large numbers of people. Schools would shut down, the companies as well, so the students and everybody would go out into the streets, and there was this wish to express love the people had for Tito by showing that a large number of people were in the streets to greet him. However, in addition to that, there were some individuals who insulted Tito by writing various slogans, and who expressed a negative attitude towards him, which was a result of the Albanian influence, where at the time Hoxha was praised and Tito was considered a revisionist with respect to the communist system in power in Albania. And the demonstrations that were organised then and later were mostly of the Marxist-Leninist character.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I want to ask Mr. Jokanovic a question. How did the army deal with the demonstrations in 1968, and in particular, were there any injuries? Was there any loss of life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The army of Yugoslavia was not used to break up the demonstrations, nor was it used for -- nor was the power and force used. The army was there just to demonstrate its force and to have a psychological effect insofar as the vehicles passed through and the army was used to secure various facilities. At the time, the demonstrators were not ready to clash with the army. They did not want to provoke the army, and there was quite a different situation with the police. I don't know if I answered your question sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you did. So the demonstrations did not last very long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in 1968, they didn't last long. But when the military forces appeared, especially in places where the demonstrations were larger and more aggressive, these demonstrations were suppressed. Tito was still alive, and his speeches are well known, when he addressed the public and said, "Let not the enemies of our system think that we have thrown a spear into the thorns," and he said that Enver Hoxha should stop wielding a rusty sword from the outside throughout Kosovo. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the -- what were the developments in the province concerning the promotion or the spread of autonomy after World War II?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the 1946 constitution, the province, which was called at the time the Autonomous Region of Kosovo and Metohija, while Vojvodina was a province. The 1963 constitution, however, then renamed the region into a province. So it became an autonomous province. Then in the amendments of 1968 and 1971, the position of the province was expanded in terms of expanding its authorities and functions so that later this was then rounded off in the constitution of 1974. The 1974 constitution gave the province practically all of the functions which the republics had. Not all of them but practically all of them in the Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jokanovic. Did the demonstrations in 1968 produce some kind of effect on the position of the province?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did have an effect in that sense, because in order to stabilise the situation in Kosovo on a more permanent basis, which could be heard in a lot of meetings, the demonstrators' demands were met, or some of those demands were met, so that those amendments of 1968, 1969, and 1971 practically met, not all but quite a lot of, those demands, giving a broader autonomy and making the province more and more equal to a republic. And in 1969, a decision of the Socialist Alliance of Yugoslavia permitted the use of the national flag to the Albanians, and that national flag was identical to the state flag of the Peoples Republic of Albania. Before that, it was not allowed to put the flag up. And those who did that usually did that on the 28th for their national holiday, and those people were fined. The use of the flag after that became quite widespread, and it served to satisfy feelings of national belongingness. There was a lot of abuse in the use of this national flag which was often used in order to provoke other people in the province, primarily Serbs, Montenegrins, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do I remember rightly, Mr. Jokanovic, this was not the traditional national flag of the Albanians but the flag of the neighbouring state of Albania? But you know this better than I do. As far as I remember, the difference between the two was the traditional flag has the two-headed eagle, black on a red background, and the neighbouring country's flag on top of that was identical but also had a five-pointed star on top. So they didn't adopt their traditional national flag but the neighbouring country's flag.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was the state flag of the Republic of Albania, with the two-headed eagle and the five-pointed star. If there are any problems about that, I could provide more details about the way the flag looked. There were attempts to change something in that flag to place the Yugoslav tricolour banner in the corner, indicating that these Albanians were in Yugoslavia, but this was something that was not accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we don't have time to spend so much on the flag, but you know so much about the former Yugoslavia and the situation in Kosovo, and it would take us a long time to go through all of that. What were the powers of Serbia in the province?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The constitution of 1974 practically denied Serbia all rights in Kosovo. The province became practically equal to the republic, both the province of Kosovo and the province of Vojvodina. There were only two differences: One was that the constitution in Serbia had Article 300, making for some singular or united solutions for the whole of the republic; and the second was that the Council of States and Republics had 12 delegates while the number of deputies from the provinces were eight. This was a symbolic difference in the numbers, but the rights that these delegations had were absolutely the same, both in the federal Chamber, there were 30 and 20 deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jokanovic. At that time, and now we're talking about the period after 1968, 1974, when all of these rights were changed, were there any pressures towards Serbs, Montenegrins, Turks, Romas, Goranians, and what was the attitude towards the Albanian population?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: After these demonstrations, Serbs, Montenegrins, and other non-Albanians had a feeling of uncertainty, quite rightly. This appeared because there were pressures towards the moving out of Serbs and Montenegrins. These were direct and indirect pressures. So these demonstrations from 1968 disrupted the interethnic relations and caused people to move out. This was a negative consequence. And also there were different forms of pressures going in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the pressures and the violence which occurred against Serbs, Montenegrins, Muslims, Turks, Romas, did Serbia have an obligation to protect the rights and freedoms of all of its citizens throughout its territory? Was that one of its constitutional duties, including the province? And also, that constitutional order, did it also have the means to fulfil this duty?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: According to its own constitution, Serbia was obliged to protect the rights of the working people and the citizens throughout the territory of the republic. There was such a provision in the Serbian constitution. However, the Republic of Serbia did not have the instruments nor the authority to protect these rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if I could interrupt briefly. That question started, "In view of the pressures and the violence which occurred against Serbs ..." Now, I don't recollect you speaking about violence against Serbs. Have you mentioned that so far?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean here while I'm testifying? Are you thinking about violence against Serbs and Croats and the pressure to have them move out? This started from the early 1960s and became more intense after 1968, and then increased even more after 1971. First of all, this pressure was directed against Serbs and Montenegrins but also towards others, towards Turks. Turks from Kosovo also moved out. I can give you specific example. A village near Gnjilane, near Kosovo, called Dobrcane, which was exclusively populated by Turks had its own elementary school, eight-year elementary school, where classes were in Turkish. Later, there were no Turks there at all because they had all moved to Turkey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did they move out?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: This was a gradual process. There was no collective movement of the population, but it was family by family; one family left, followed by another family. And this happened in a period from 1968 up until sometime in the 1980s, and I think until up to about some ten years ago, perhaps there were two or three Turkish families left in that village, which in the meantime had integrated through marriage and in other ways, attended school in Albanian, and were integrated into a different kind of life in comparison to the earlier period when the village was exclusively inhabited by Turkish nationals.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Milosevic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no need to keep turning the microphone off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, could you please tell me what the situation was in the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The judiciary in Yugoslavia was organised in Yugoslavia in the republics and in the provinces in exactly the same way. The judiciary functions were at the level of the province. The province had municipal courts, district courts, and supreme courts. There was the Supreme Court of Kosovo. That was the highest instance in order to achieve citizens' rights and to resolve different disputes and questions from civil law and other kinds of law, so that those citizens who felt their rights were violated, according to the law and the constitution, could not resort to Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond the courts of Serbia, they had to remain in the provincial court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jokanovic. I have to cut you off; we do not have too much time. Could you please tell us what the situation was with the executive and administrative powers or authorities.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The constitution --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we all understand the position regarding the constitution, but what was the actual situation?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The executive authority was completely under the provincial organs. The provincial bodies were the only ones in charge of implementing the laws, the provincial laws and republican laws, if a law applied throughout the whole territory, as well as federal laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In light of what you have said, that the provincial authorities were exclusively authorised, how do you look at the assertion in the following paragraph of the so-called indictment? Paragraph 80 states: "Due to political turmoil, on 3rd of March, 1989 the SFRY Presidency declared that the situation in the province had deteriorated and had become a threat to the constitution, integrity and sovereignty of the country. The government then imposed special measures which assigned responsibility for public security to the federal government instead of the government of Serbia". Please pay attention to what I have just quoted. This is an excerpt from this document. So "... assigned responsibility for public security to the federal government instead of the government of Serbia." End of quote. Could you please give us your comments on what I have just read to you.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The first part seems to be all right. These special measures were introduced and the political and security situation did deteriorate, but this last part is completely incorrect because the federal government could not assign as they said that there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. The full sentence states as follows: "The government then imposed special measures which assigned responsibility for public security to the federal government instead of the government of Serbia." So the federal government transferred the responsibility for public security from the government of Serbia to the federal government.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it could not have done that, because Serbia did not have authority in that area. It could only have transferred this responsibility from the provincial organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Serbia did not have the authority nor implemented the authority which the federal government could have transferred from Serbia to the federal government.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It did not have those powers. If the Honourable Court allows me, I could say a little bit more about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you believe that it is important, please go ahead, but please try to be brief.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to mention one fact. When there were demonstrations in 1981, the Serbian police offered to help the police of Kosovo, but the provincial organs did not permit Serbian police to help its colleagues. So that the police of Serbia, for days, was near the administrative border of Kosovo, in a place called Rudare, and was waiting for the outcome of the situation. Only later was it allowed to a part of these forces to come in, but not as part -- as Serbian forces but as part of the joint Yugoslav forces comprising Slovenians, Croats, people from -- members of the police force from Vojvodina, Macedonia, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what you said about the government imposing special measures, assigning the responsibility from the government of Serbia to the federal government regarding security measures is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is incorrect because it is something that did not exist and could not have been transferred or assigned to somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'd like to be clear about this. Who had the authority, the constitutional authority, for public security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The constitutional authority for security in Kosovo and Metohija lay with the organs of Kosovo and Metohija in accordance with the Kosovo constitution, with its laws, and in accordance with the constitution of Yugoslavia. Because the implementation of all the laws and the preservation of peace and order was under the jurisdiction of the province bodies, the provincial secretariat for internal affairs and the provincial security service, which was separate from the Serbian service of the same kind. It was independent, and it had an equal standing as the Serbian Security Service and the internal affairs services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. So what you say is that it would not have been legally possible for the federal government to transfer the powers to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Mr. Robinson. I quoted -- very well. Yes. It will be clear. I would like to make it clear. I quoted here their paper here which they called the indictment, which also has some more serious untruths than this one, but it says: "The government then imposed its special measures which assigned responsibility for public security to the federal government instead of the government of Serbia." But this is not true, because the government of Serbia did not carry out any functions in the first place for the federal government to be able to take over these services upon itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this clear? So it was not in a position to assign functions to somebody else which Serbia did not have in the first place. It did not have them and it did not implement them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That was the constitutional de jure position, but did it in fact happen?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, de facto it had no powers either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This de jure situation was also the de facto situation with one single difference; namely, after the 1981 demonstrations, the federal authorities established joint police forces, taking forces from all the republics and the province of Vojvodina in order to assist the Kosovo organs. Within those joint forces, there were also forces from Serbia under the command of the chief of that staff who was appointed by the competent ministry. So it was not within the competency of Serbia. I don't know if this is clear enough. I can try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, did you, as provincial secretary for legislation and general administration, because that's the post you occupied at the time, take part in the work on the harmonisation of those laws under Article 300 of the Serbian constitution? In other words, to cut a long story short, it was the only article of the constitution which enabled the Republic of Serbia to exercise certain functions on the entirety of its territory on the condition of agreement with the province. So even that provision was not quite enabling for Serbia, but under Article 300, we were at least in a position to reach agreement with the province.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: From 1978 to 1982, I was the provincial secretary for legislation and administration. Pursuant to Article 300, some issues were included that were regulated in a uniform way for the entire territory of Serbia. However, this Article 300 was rather vague and generally phrased so that these issues that were uniformly regulated applied only to the basic principles and uniform fundaments, and it was very difficult to determine exactly how far these basic principles went. And as a result, the negotiations with the representatives of Vojvodina and Kosovo were difficult, lengthy, and often unsuccessful. Agreement was very difficult to reach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, before going further, if you could remind me of the content of the Article 300 of the Serbian constitution. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have the Article 300 of the constitution of Serbia with me, but it enumerates issues that may be uniformly regulated within the Republic of Serbia. However, this Article 300 was unclear, vague, and phrased in very general terms. So any attempt to interpret it resulted in diametrically opposed positions. In controversy, in other words. And may I add to this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. If you could clarify the meaning of "uniformly regulated within Republic of Serbia." If you would elaborate on that more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can ask a question of this witness, or a set of questions. I think this will be a more efficient way of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This Article 300, was it the only article in the constitution of Serbia which allowed something to be uniformly regulated within the whole republic?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was also Article 305, but it only provided for the possibility of similar or equal regulation in the republic and the province.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Under that Article 300, the parliament of Serbia could regulate certain things in general terms on the whole territory. However, that had to be agreed with the representatives of the province before it is passed?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me pick up on the question by Judge Kwon. For instance, the citizenship of the Republic of Serbia, because there was no citizenship of the province; right?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the citizenship of the Republic of Serbia, they insisted that they should decide in Kosovo and Metohija about the citizenship of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I was involved for a long time in discussions and debates about this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please say whether it is correct or not and then tell us the rest.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: It is correct that the provincial authorities demanded that they should decide on the citizenship of the Republic of Serbia proceeding from what I said before, namely, that it is the provincial authorities who were in charge of the enforcement of all laws, including this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So tell me, what was the point? This is a very general point: What was the point in the insistence of provincial authorities that the province should decide about the citizenship of the Republic of Serbia relating to the citizens on its territory?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: There were two main reasons. They wanted to demonstrate that the province was practically a republic. They wanted to put a mark of equality between the province and the republic. That was one reason. The second reason was that if the province had been enabled to do that, then they would have been able to resolve certain issues, including this one. They would have been enabled -- they would have been able to give citizenship to some immigrants who had come to Kosovo during the anti-fascist war, to Kosovo from Albania and remained there, and a variety of other immigrants.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this second objective was very pragmatic: They wanted to have competency over their citizenship of Serbia in order to give citizenship to various immigrants from Albania.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely where our differences lay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that correct?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That was one of the reasons. The first reason, as I said, was they wanted to demonstrate their powers as a state, and the second was that they wanted to decide as a province in the province who would have citizenship and who wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when did Albanians start to immigrate into Kosovo? Just let me say that I have no historical background to this question. When did this immigration of Albanians into Kosovo begin? Let us skip this great number of Albanians who were moved to Kosovo by Mussolini and who remained there after the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: After the comintern resolution of 1948 and the famous "No" that Tito said to Stalin when he was proclaimed a revisionist, a considerable number of Albanians moved to Kosovo, fleeing this Stalinist system. They came one by one but also with their entire families, with whole herds of sheep and a lot of equipment, and they were very cordially welcomed because it was in the political interest --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. They came en masse in this period. Please answer me with a yes or no, and then if there is an explanation to follow, give it later. Did they come en masse?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Not at the beginning, but later, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the hard-line regime of Enver Hoxha and the police control over the citizenry in Albania, was it possible to easily cross without any problem the Albanian border with whole families, furniture, herds of cattle, et cetera? Was that possible or not?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that they were moved to Kosovo and Metohija in a planned way also by the Enver Hoxha regime?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: That was tolerated. I don't know if there was a plan behind it, but it was tolerated, because they did come and they were welcomed. I don't know if the border was controlled, then there could have also been a plan behind it, but they did come en masse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said they were welcomed, well-received in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They also received some allowances and financial support, and the objective was to integrate them as fast as possible into the Kosovo society, to give them employment, and there were even instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify one thing. Is it true that the then-government of Kosovo, such as the Ministry of Internal Affairs, for instance, or correct me, whichever other ministry, repurchased estates of Serbs and Montenegrins who moved out of Kosovo and gave them free of charge to Albanians who had moved into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and if you allow me one more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Either leading or tendentious. It may not matter because it may be that had we seen a statement of the witness in advance some of these matters would be non-contentious, but there is a balance to be drawn between leading questions that are acceptable and those that really may go to the heart of the issue. So the last one, for example, where there was a suggestion that these things were repurchased and given free of charge to Albanians, it's not something I know about and therefore it shouldn't really be asked in that form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have discussed this before, Mr. Milosevic. You're not to ask leading questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, there are many things in this wide world that your wisdom does not even imagine, Dear Horatio. I was trying to quote Shakespeare. I don't even expect you to know anything about this. That's one thing. And second, it is not my obligation to take prior statements of a witness and disclose them to Mr. Nice. He should not be wasting my time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I stopped you because you're making a speech. The rules here prohibit leading questions. And, Mr. Milosevic, there is a matter that I should bring to your attention: You're examining this witness, and the purpose of the examination is to assist the Chamber. It's not a private dialogue between yourself and the witness. The constitutional issues are important issues, the question of the distribution of powers between the federal government and the provinces. You ought to have had the constitution here to show us and Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond have it translated. So, for example, I'm interested in seeing what powers are set out in Article 300. The purpose of your examination is to persuade us, and you ought to have had that here. I think -- is it probably -- is it an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Unfortunately -- an exhibit and I think the exhibit number is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is 526, tab 1. I think that's the exhibit. But the articles that are under consideration are not included in the part of the document that's been prepared as an exhibit thus far, or certainly are not in English. They may be, conceivably, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if you could check Exhibit 132. It says Constitution of Serbia, but it's a later version maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The point is, Mr. Milosevic, in presenting your evidence and in examining the witness, you must have documents available for us so that when he speaks of Article 300, we can be looking at it and looking at it in the English. That is the way you will strengthen your case. The presentation of your case would be advanced tremendously if you do it in the right way. My colleague and myself were just saying to ourselves privately that we are somewhat at a loss in understanding the constitutional points that have been raised because we don't have the documents in front of us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, you will allow that I believe that the issue of the language of the constitution cannot be in dispute. It is the wording of the constitution that was passed and in force at the time, and if you need it, I will tender it as an exhibit through one of the following witnesses. We have Professor Ratko Markovic coming, and I'll introduce that text through him. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You ought to have -- you ought to have introduced it through this witness, because he's giving evidence that relates to the constitution. Don't wait for Professor Ratko Markovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In order to avoid leading questions, Mr. Jokanovic, how were Albanian immigrants received at the time?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: They were well received. When farmers from Albania moved in, who couldn't find jobs in enterprises, it was necessary to repurchase land so that they could engage in farming. Therefore, land was repurchased from Serbs and Montenegrins who were moving out of Kosovo, and this entire land, complete with equipment, was given to immigrants who came to Albania. I'll give you an example. In my neighbouring village, Grmovo, the village called Drobes, the land was repurchased from the Nikoletic family and another family. They live nowadays in Kraljevo, whereas these two villages are inhabited by those immigrants who came from Albania, and the funding was provided through the provincial Secretariat for Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can I note then that you said that the police of Kosovo repurchased arable land from Serbs and Montenegrins and gave it free of charge to Albanian immigrants who came to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The contracts were made out between the republican -- sorry, the provincial Secretariat for Internal Affairs and these immigrant farmers. It was probably budgetary funding that was paid out through the provincial secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jokanovic. I will quote another paragraph from this so-called indictment. Paragraph 75. It goes as follows: "During the 1980s, Serbs voiced concern about discrimination against them by the Kosovo Albanian led provincial government while Kosovo Albanians voiced concern about economic underdevelopment and dependence and called for a greater political liberalisation and republican status for Kosovo. From 1981 onwards, Kosovo Albanians staged demonstrations which were suppressed by the SFRY military and police forces of Serbia." All right. So I quoted this verbatim. Could you please answer and tell me what you know about this.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: As for the discrimination mentioned in the first sentence, that's a mild term. There were various pressures, attacks, crimes against property, against person, beatings, rapes, and so on. As for the second claim, that Albanians sought greater political liberalisation, I don't think this is a proper term. What they wanted was secession from Serbia. They wanted Kosovo to become a republic. And as for the demonstrations from 1981 onwards being suppressed by the military and police from Serbia, that's not true. The army did demonstrate its force but never had any clashes with the demonstrators at the time because, as I said, the demonstrators tried not to provoke the army and not to even mention the police of Serbia, because as I've said before, the Serbian police had no competencies in Kosovo. Later on, when the joint forces from all other republics were established, yes, they were present in Kosovo up until 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if I could be clear about something then in regard to that answer. If all they wanted was to become a republic, and if as a province they had all the powers of a republic, what was the point of the demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To secede entirely from Serbia and become an independent state, which is their current goal nowadays as well, the main objective of political forces and political parties in Kosovo nowadays. They didn't want to be either within Serbia or within Yugoslavia. That was their goal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I misunderstood your answer, because I assumed by "republic" you were referring to a Yugoslav republic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if you could explain more about the joint forces you mentioned from all other republics. Could you elaborate on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. When in 1981 Serbian police was not allowed to assist their colleagues in Kosovo and Metohija police, they looked for a solution how to suppress demonstrations, because Kosovo police could not deal with it alone. Therefore, a compromise was found to engage members of police in all other republics and provinces, meaning Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Macedonia, and Vojvodina. I can name specific cases where what police members were deployed. In Lipljan municipality there were policemen from Vojvodina. In my municipality we had policemen from Croatia. In other municipalities there were policemen from Bosnia and Herzegovina. So these joined forces helped the Kosovo police in order to stabilise the situation and not allow any further destruction of property and everything else that comes along with demonstrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which is to say, Mr. Jokanovic, based on this quotation where I read out their text to you about police forces of Serbia suppressing those demonstrations, that is not true; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't want this to be taken as a leading question, therefore I said that the forces of Serbia were not allowed to go to Kosovo. They could only go to Kosovo if they were joined by forces, police forces, from all other republics. Therefore, it was not the Serbian police who suppressed the demonstrations, no. It was the Kosovo police and joint police forces from all other republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jokanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When were the police forces established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These joint forces were established after 1981, because the demonstrations in 1981 could not be suppressed by Kosovo police alone. And therefore, if I remember correctly, on the 1st of March the competent organ within the province issued a decision to involve the army and to have tanks roll through the streets. And in 1981, the army did do that. The tanks came out into the streets, and the key Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond organs in Kosovo were involved because Kosovo police was unable to deal with it. In the evening on that day, planes flew over Pristina, and the freedom of movement was limited. I was a member of the Kosovo Council at the time, and I can show you the ID that I had issued to me during that period of time allowing me freedom of movement. Would you like me to show you that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead. That was the ID that you were issued with at that time.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where I should put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can put it on the ELMO. The usher will help you.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: We can see what it says here, that this is an official ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Leje zyrtare" means official pass. You have the text in Albanian then in Serbian after that. Then you can see my name, and then underneath it says that I'm involved in executing certain tasks assigned to me by the Executive Council of the Assembly of the province of Kosovo, as a result of which "he should be given access and freedom of movement." There were some announcements that demonstrators wanted to take up key facilities in Kosovo so that even as a member of the Executive Council of Kosovo, I could not have entered any important building without this special pass.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you need to take -- to further examine in ID, to have it tendered into evidence, or is this sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, Mr. Jokanovic, what was the scope and what was the nature of the demonstrations of Albanians in 1981?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The demonstrations in 1981, in view of the numbers of people participating and the aggression expressed were much broader than the 1968 demonstrations but can still be qualified as a continuity of action, because the demands and slogans were the same: "Kosovo Republic" and "Unification," except that in 1981 there were many more people participating in the demonstrations and more aggression was expressed. So that in 1981, there were victims both among demonstrators and law enforcement personnel. I can even give you the numbers, if you're interested. Nine demonstrators were killed in the demonstrations, two members of the organ of the internal affairs, and dozens of policemen were also injured, as were the demonstrators. Several vehicles were set on fire, shop windows were broken, so there was quite a lot of property damage. The demonstrations became most aggressive on the 2nd April of 1981 when the army was called to come in to protect the key facilities and institutions within the province.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where were the fiercest demonstrations held?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: In Pristina on the 2nd of April, because in addition to demonstrations organised in other cities, on that day, from other cities, from Podujevo and other towns, demonstrators converged in Pristina, and it was very difficult to stop them. The forces of Kosovo police were unable to stop them. And it wasn't until the army was involved to come in and secure the key facilities and the planes that flew over the town that the demonstrations were calmed down. That was towards the evening, around 8.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Jokanovic. What was the attitude of political organs with respect to demonstrations? When I say "political organs," I'm referring both to provincial, to republic, and federal organs. What was their attitude?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, the attitude was similar to the one in 1968. They tried to cover up, to present this as a rebellion of students who were unhappy with their accommodation and so on. However, when the demonstrations escalated and when the leadership saw that their functions, posts, and privileges were jeopardised, then the organs of the province started condemning those demonstrations in very severe terms. One of the worst qualifications in the then-system was the qualifications of counterrevolution. One of the closest associates of Tito was so fierce in his condemnations that he said that these demonstrators were the worst enemy of the Albanian people and that they were thugs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And there are documents which can prove that?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And then other organs also joined in condemning the demonstrations. The Province Committee, Central Committee of the League of Communists, and they also wanted the provincial leadership to be made accountable for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was Enver Hoxha mentioned during those demonstrations, or any other Albanian figures?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, some historical figures were mentioned. The unification of Kosovo was mentioned. Then there was the slogan "Kosovo Republic." So these 1981 demonstrations were identical to the 1968 demonstrations in the demands expressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, Serbia had no competencies, nor could Serbia have suppressed those demonstrations.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Serbia had no competencies, and it could not have suppressed the demonstrations, which cause great dissatisfaction among the citizenry who asked publicly, what was the role of Serbia? Could Serbia defend its territory integrity, its citizens, state and private property? And it was precisely then that demands and criticism were voiced, saying that the constitution ought to be amended, this constitution that does not allow the republic to protect its citizens and the property in its own territory and to protect its own territorial integrity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Jokanovic. So the paragraph 75 is this bit that says that the police forces of Serbia suppressed the demonstrations is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It's incorrect because the police forces of Serbia did not suppress it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You explained to us how the issue of suppressing the demonstrations was resolved. Were you specific enough when you said who was in command of these joint police forces that came to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the name of the person who was in command, but he was someone from Croatia, whereas Franc, a Slovene, was in charge of Special Police Unit, he was in charge of an action which -- an operation in the village of Prekaze where some people shut themselves in a house and the police had to deal with that. The fire was opened. So this special unit, Special Police Unit from Slovenia, was led by the person, a Slovene named Franz. It was a violent operation, helicopters were called in, and those who put up resistance were fired upon by the police. The fire was opened from the helicopter as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was in Prekaze in 1981?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in Prekaze again in 1998, fire was opened against the police and there was a conflict except that some aspects were different. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember the first case in Prekaze because I was living in Kosovo at the time, and as a member of the Executive Council, together with some other leaders, I went to that village and I saw the house involved. And as for the other instance that you mentioned, I didn't go there personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm not going to put any further questions, but let me just tell you that the second case in Prekaze is identical to the first one, practically a twin of the first one. But please tell me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, could you give me the year again? The transcript says 1998. The year in Prekaze.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What Mr. Jokanovic described in Prekaze happened in 1981, whereas I mentioned Prekaze and the event that took place there in 1998. The same event happened there in 1998 when the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond group led by Adem Jashari was liquidated. The same group that fired on police members, and a lot of citizens were killed there. That was in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In 1981, the special police of the federal -- the Special Police Unit of the federal police was engaged there, and it was under the command of a Slovene officer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was called Special Police Unit there, and today it would have been called Anti-Terrorist Unit or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, please tell me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, on the subject you've been dealing with, when you talked, Mr. Jokanovic about fire being opened, or someone opening fire in 1981, were you referring to the police being attacked or were you referring to the police themselves opening fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1981, firearms were used both by the demonstrators. The demonstrators were the first to use weapons. According to the statement of Stane Dolenc, a Slovene, who was the person most responsible for security in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, you're a politician, and you speak in general terms. You said, for example, that Stane Dolenc was the most responsible for. Why don't you say that Stane Dolenc was the federal police minister? This is much clearer to them than if you say that he was the most responsible. Both statements are correct, but it's much more specific if you say that he was the federal police minister.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. He was the federal police minister, he was a Slovene, and he held other important functions later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was going to say that the witness should have the opportunity, if he wishes, to complete his answer to my question. I resent being interrupted by the accused and a witness who is answering a question of mine being interrupted in the course of it. Now, is there anything else you wish to say in answer to my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the 1981 demonstrations, firearms were used by the demonstrators and police as well, but in response. Nine demonstrators were killed, and two policemen. In the village of Prekaze, weapons were used by an Albanian who barricaded himself inside the house and then opened fire from the house. The police surrounded the house and made a shelter for police members. They did not want to engage in combat inside the house. And then Special Police Unit was called in under the command of the Slovene police officer who liquidated this house from which resistance was put up and from which the fire was opened on police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have led evidence about the demonstrations in 1968, demonstrations in 1981, and I think you're now going to deal with 1998, but we're going to take the break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Milosevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, these events of 1981, and I'm thinking of the demonstrations which you've already talked about a lot, how did they reflect upon the lives of Serbs and Montenegrins and other non-Albanians in the province?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Very negatively, because inter-ethnic relations were disrupted even further. Insecurity was created, lack of hope, and this reflected very negatively upon the overall situation in Kosovo, because Serbs, even after that, were exposed to various forms of pressure exerted against themselves, their property. Their fields were destroyed. Graveyards were destroyed. The Pec monastery was set on fire. And there were also provocations, insults, attacks. There was an attack at the -- the Orthodox bishop at the time, and there was also an attack on a priest in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember any incidents involving killings? Was any of that happening?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were some killings. I remember certain cases which were particularly unusual. There was a killing in the village of Mec near Djakovica. There was the only Serbian house in that village. And upon instructions of the presidents of the -- of the president of the Presidency of Kosovo at the time went to visit that family because that person had written letters to the highest organs of the federation, the Republic of Serbia and Kosovo, that he's afraid that he would be killed imminently. And with another Albanian who happened to be the president of the Commission for Complaints, went to visit that person and then went to the municipality of Djakovica and asked the municipal Secretariat for Internal Affairs to extend protection for this person. Unfortunately, very soon after that, Miodrag Saric was killed in his yard right next to his house, because he had already prepared material in order to rebuild and renovate his old house. I had visited his old house. There was another case of Danilo Milancic in Samodreza near Vucitrn. A young man was killed. Before that, his father was killed also. These are cases which were covered a lot in the press. There was also the case of Martinovic in Gnjilane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Jokanovic. When did you hear the term "ethnically pure Kosovo" for the first time?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that term in official documents of the provincial political bodies, in official documents of the political organs of Yugoslavia. This term was used following 1981, stating that the objective of the separatists and Albanian nationalists was to create an ethnically pure Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell us how the organs of the province, the republic, and the SFRY placed themselves in relation to these problems of harassment, moving out, and so on.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Up until 1981, this was a taboo topic. Nobody discussed it, and it was a problem that everybody ignored. From 1981, this problem was something that the provincial organs, the republican organs, and the federal organs all had to deal with, and they assessed this problem and decided upon specific measures, and they adopted conclusions in order to prevent the moving out of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who made these measures?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The Assembly of Kosovo adopted these measures. The Federal Assembly adopted the measures also, as well as the Executive Council or the Assembly of Serbia. Measures were adopted by other political organs in the League of Communists and the Socialist Alliance. So this question became topical and it was mentioned in numerous documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Jokanovic. Did all these measures stop the wave of emigration from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, they did not. These measures did not yield the expected results. When the implementation of the measures was assessed the term that was used was "insufficient activity," "inefficacy," and also "opportunism" in the implementation of these measures. So that this emigration from Kosovo continued even after the adoption of these measures, and it affected all the administrative organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did the Serbs and Montenegrins feel protected after these measures were adopted?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, they did not feel protected. After 1981, the unrest was even greater. And then in subsequent years, starting from 1982, the so-called rallies of Serbs and Montenegrins began who began to rally together in the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond places where they lived in order to point out the problems that they were facing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say for different reasons, which reasons are you thinking of? What is the nature of the -- why did they rally together?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: When a fight broke out, there was a rape, someone was arrested, or even if there was a visit by any member of the Commission for Complaints. There was such a commission comprising all the federal organs which toured all the different municipalities and reviewed all the complaints made by the citizens. So when this commission would, for example, come to visit my municipality of Vitina, we would have a large number of people who would come together in order to state what their problems were, in order to acquaint the people who had come to visit them with the problems that they were facing. So these rallies took place in several locations around Kosovo. And when this, as well, did not yield the expected results, Serbs decided to go and take their complaints to Belgrade, to go to Belgrade to ask for help and justice. They went to visit all the republican bodies because they were disappointed with the conduct of the republican organs, because they felt that it was up to the republic to protect them. Then they would instead go to the Federal Assembly and to see officials who were members of the federal bodies. There were several such visits to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the situation at the University of Pristina at the time? Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The university in Pristina was actually an outpost of the Belgrade University, and then first faculties were formed and then a university was formed later. But this university was gradually turning into primarily an Albanian university, while classes in Serbian were being suppressed. And professors were complaining. I would see them, and I would hear the series of problems that they were facing in their work. This was the problem of majorisation and the problem of keys. And this keys policy was referring to quotas during -- when people were enrolling, quotas taking into account the national structure, and it brought the Serbs into an unequal position. It was positive discrimination. So then these classes were just classes that had to be there and were meant to be gradually phased out. There were fewer and fewer people from Kosovo who spoke Albanian who were moving out, so that classes in Serbian were becoming more and more threatened. Up until 1980-something, over 60 per cent of teachers from Kosovo had left and had moved to other places in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation with the economic development of Kosovo at the time?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: From the late 1960s, and that's the period of my direct participation in such work, particularly from 1970, when I became the president of the municipality, the economy of Kosovo grew very quickly and dynamically, and this area used to be the least developed area in the former Yugoslavia. So there was practically a rebirth of Kosovo that took place over a period of two decades, and the progress they made in such a short time would be something that other nations would perhaps need much more time to achieve. It was a place where there were a lot of illiterate people, there was practically no industry, there were no schools. So in this period, thanks to the fund for the development of undeveloped regions, a large number of facilities were built, economic facilities, also the infrastructure was built, and there were a lot of social services that were developed. In my municipality during my mandate, more factories were built -- several factories were built, and the number of employees in those factories doubled. I remember out of 3.800 workers who were there when I took on office, when I left my office, there were 9.000 workers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear Mr. Milosevic's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first problem that I directly faced were after the demonstrations in 1981, because amongst, other things which I mentioned, you could hear more and more criticism about the constitution, and there were more and more suggestions to change or amend the constitution. And also saying that the constitution itself, perhaps, was among the causes of problems in Kosovo. In 1980, already they talked about the essential changes that had to be made to the amendments in 1981. This was something that was dealt with by the federal, republican, and provincial organs. In 1982 and 1983, the conclusions of the Central Committee of LCY of Yugoslavia were presented in an analysis in order to achieve unity in the Republic of Serbia where all the different aspects were pointed out how to achieve unity and what the problems were in that and what had to be changed in certain regulations and what had to be stated more specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please tell us when the work on the draft amendments to the constitution of Serbia began, and how long did this work take?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to talk about the things that I participated in directly. For the first time, I took part in a meeting of the Presidency work group, the Presidency of Serbia, together with my colleagues, Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment. What was your function? On what basis did you participate in this working group of the Presidency of Serbia; as a representative of Kosovo or were you invited by the Presidency of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I was a representative of Kosovo because I was a member of the Kosovo Presidency, in charge of constitutional questions and the political systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many of you from Kosovo took part in this work?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Two of us. The vice-president of the Executive Council, who was also in charge with constitutional questions and legal matters, and then later we had a professor from the Pristina University. Both of these people were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This was in 1986 in Boticeva Street at the government of the Republic of Serbia. This first meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me who presided over this meeting.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The meeting was scheduled and presided over by the president of the Presidency of Serbia at the time, Ivan Stambolic. And from Vojvodina there was a member of the Presidency. It was my colleague, his name was Vujadinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was the composition from Vojvodina also ethnically mixed?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: From Vojvodina the composition was the same. This Vujadinovic person was probably a Serb or a Montenegrin, I don't know. There was also a secretary for legal matters. I don't know what his ethnicity was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So work on this draft amendment began in 1986. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this is what you participated in?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1986 I participated as a member of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me now whether this working group which was formed and this constitutional commission which was formed had to consult with their grassroots, with their electorate.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: This was essential. We were not there as free shooters representing our own opinion.
