Before the meetings and after the meetings which we had as a group, we were obliged to inform the Presidency of Kosovo, the constitutional commission of Kosovo, the Presidency of the Kosovo provincial council. They would form their views based on our positions, and then we would convey these positions back again. We would try to coordinate and harmonise this position. There was a large number of meetings on each particular matter discussed at the level of the province and also in order to reach a consensus with our constituency. There were also meetings with representatives of Serbia and Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So work on the draft that you had and work at the commission which was presided over by Ivan Stambolic began in 1986.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The drafting of proposals began in 1986, and that was the direction and the scale of changes. So this proposition or proposal Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond discussed about the things that needed to be changed. And then when this proposal was adopted, then this work was transferred to the constitutional commission of the Republic of Serbia and such commissions of Kosovo and Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was this transferred to the constitutional commission?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That was in 1987. Here in paragraph 79 of this paper that I'm quoting to you from, which was prepared by the other side, it states: "In early 1989" -- so this is what it states here: "In early 1989, the Serbian Assembly proposed amendments to the constitution of Serbia which would strip Kosovo of most of its autonomous powers, including control of the police, educational and economic policy, and choice -- as well as its veto powers over further changes to the constitution of Serbia." Please, could you comment on that.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to be as brief as possible. The constitutional amendments were worked on for a long time. It took three years to harmonise positions. In 1989, a draft was adopted by the Assembly, and this was then put out for public debate. So after a long time of hard work, which included all of the organs of the Vojvodina and Kosovo provinces as well as the republican organs. So by that draft, the province of Kosovo was not stripped of its autonomous powers. All of its jurisdiction or powers remained. The amendments just restored several functions to Serbia in the sphere of national defence, internal affairs, but not the entirety of internal affairs, only those pertaining to the security of the Republic of Serbia as a whole. And there was also a procedure established of joint activities with the provincial organs, but the other questions remained in the jurisdiction of the province. This draft in no way changed the position of the province within the federation. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well, Mr. Jokanovic. So this passage that I quoted to you stripped the majority of its autonomous powers, including control of the police, educational and economic policy. From what you say, then, it seems that this is not true.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is not true, especially the part pertaining to veto powers. I didn't respond to that. The draft amendment, or when the amendments were adopted, there was no right of veto. The veto power was substituted with a complex procedure to change the constitution of Serbia. Instead of veto powers, which deprived Serbia of its basic constitutional function which every republic had, the amendments provided for a complex procedure, meaning that if consensus is not achieved, the Assembly cannot effect a change. This is postponed for six months, and then within that period if consensus is not achieved, then -- or if one of the provinces is opposed to that, then the Assembly of Serbia cannot adopt these changes again, and then these changes can be effected only through a referendum. But there was a solution found. A way out was found from a veto through this complex procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And all these things that were done, were they done in such a way as to include actively the political leadership at the level of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: That work could not have been done and changes would not have been possible without the direct and active involvement of federal bodies, especially the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, which had the most authority and was the integrating -- the greatest integrating factor in the country. The positions expressed by the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia expressed at various sessions were very important, such as the 9th, the 16th, and especially the 17th session, especially point 5, where it said that Serbia should be able to exercise its powers throughout its territory without changing the status of the province as an integral part of the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Jokanovic. You provided, among other documents, and that is an exhibit, 964, that has been provided to you timely, in English. We have a memo here saying Exhibits for Vukasin Jokanovic, item 6, document titled The Policy of the LCY in Kosovo, Pristina. It contains all these positions expressed by various republican authorities, as well as federal bodies, the bodies of Serbia, of Yugoslavia, pertaining --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the document that you have just submitted, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document of the League of Communists of Kosovo encompassing the policy of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia in Kosovo, including original records of various political meetings dealing with the issue of constitutional amendments and the situation in Kosovo in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you going to refer to specific parts of it? It's not translated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was disclosed much in advance, sufficiently in advance, and I will quote, because there is no time to dwell on it a lot, but for instance, I will quote from the record of a meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There seems to be some confusion as to whether there's translation. We have never received an English translation of this document. We have received English translations of a number of other documents, but not of this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you say it was submitted in advance for translation? How much in advance?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know, I must say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you must know. That attitude is just not acceptable. If you intend to rely on the document, you know what the general rule is: The document must be translated in one of the working languages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So as not to waste more time, may I quote from this document or not? If you say I'm not allowed to, I'll move on, ask other questions. I'm sorry this hasn't been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in light of the fact that you did submit it for translation some time ago, although we were made to understand that you were asked to identify particular passages for translation and you're not in a position to do so, but in light of that, we will allow you to refer to it if the passage is short, because it will have to be translated by the interpreters. What is the passage to which you wish to refer?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, Mr. Robinson. I will skip all the passages where I spoke, and I will quote only from page 42, the words of the then president of the Presidency of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, a Croat by ethnicity, who also participated in that meeting, and he spoke about constitutional amendments. I have only a couple of quotations. This particular Croat was not looking very kindly upon the Serbian leadership at the time. He you could say that he was even opposed. His name is Stipe Suvar, he says -- and I will try to think of the interpreters. He says: "Our main problem is that throughout these years, from the explosion of Albanian nationalism, accompanied by all those counterrevolutionary demands from 1981 onwards, we still have not made or achieved this in-depth transformation. We did not improve the situation or achieve stabilisation." And he goes on to say: "Together with Albanians, who are an overwhelming majority in the province, there live there also Serbs and Montenegrins who feel the most threatened and are indeed the most threatened, followed by Muslims, who live there in considerable numbers, as well as Romas, Croats, and all the others." Further down below, he says: "It is ludicrous to hear discussions about which nationalism is more dangerous. In Kosovo, the Albanian nationalism is 100 times more dangerous."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry to be technically difficult, but I think if we're going to be quoting or taking extracts from documents in Serbian, what we've done in the past and what probably ought to be done now is the document ought be on the overhead projector --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm not following and I'll sit down. But I think it ought to be read probably by the accused -- very well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would also appreciate it if they could hear the page number for each separate quotation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, would you identify the page numbers for each quotation so that the interpreters can follow it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did give a page number. I started with page 42. Then there is a small quotation from page 44. And I read very slowly. And this is not a meeting that took place in Serbia. It is a summit meeting of the Yugoslav leadership that was held in Pristina, and I was quoting the words of the leader of that Yugoslav summit, at that time president of the Yugoslav Presidency, Croat by ethnicity, Stipe Suvar. Now, page 46, he says that: "It is a good thing --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, could you bear in mind so that the interpreters can follow the text through ELMO, so could you check whether the ELMO shows the relevant part of the text or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the ELMO -- Mr. Jokanovic, will you please turn to page 46. That's where I am now. And this is the paragraph. The end of the first column, page 46, the then president says: "In conclusion, I think what happened in the Assembly of Serbia concerning constitutional amendments is good, as well as the way it happened. First of all, I can't understand why the Albanian masses in Kosovo seem to think that something radically changed here, because the amendments relate to five or six issues, and it is quite normal that Serbia receives competence over them as a state, even if we are not reconciling ourselves with the fact that Serbia is not composed of three states; that is, unless we are willing to reconcile ourselves with Serbia being composed of three states, that is, unless we allow two provinces to grow into states and become states." What was going on at that time at the summit level in Yugoslavia completely coincides with the description just given by Witness Jokanovic, because I asked him to what extent the political leadership of Yugoslavia was involved --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've stopped you. Ask a question of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do that, could I possibly have clarification. What is the document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the record of a summit meeting of the Yugoslav leadership held in Pristina, and the president of the Presidency of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, Dr. Stipe Suvar, from Croatia - it was Croatia's turn at the time to provide the president - spoke on this issue, and he expressed the position of the Yugoslav leadership, not the Serbian leadership. And then on page 47 -- in order to save time, I skipped my own words at that meeting, but you have it in its entirety, and you can read it. The document is titled conclusions of the Presidency of the Provincial Committee of The League of Communists of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, it was mostly Albanians in this Presidency; right?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these are conclusions of the Presidency of the provincial committee of the League of Communists of Kosovo the 28th of February 1989. Page 47, paragraph 2: "They invoke the stances taken by the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." Paragraph 5: "The Presidency of the provincial committee of the League of Communists of Kosovo --" page 48, for the benefit of the interpreters, the end of column 1. "The Presidency of the provincial committee of the League of Communists of Kosovo reiterates once again that it supports constitutional changes to the constitution of Serbia and demands that they be passed as soon as possible in order for the Republic of Serbia to be able to exercise its powers and functions on its whole territory, because these amendments do not jeopardise the autonomy of provinces or the equality among peoples and minorities." I will just want to ask you, what is the -- what was the position of the top Yugoslav authorities at that time? I quoted to you the position of the Provincial Committee from Kosovo, which was composed mostly of Albanians and presided over by an Albanian. Mr. Jokanovic, for the Assembly of Serbia to be able to pass these amendments, it was necessary to receive the approval of both provinces; is that so?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it necessary to have the approval of the Republic of Serbia for provincial assemblies to pass amendments?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Serbia's approval was not necessary. Provinces could change their constitutions independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, we will now move on to very specific issues, questions, because as you just confirmed, you were at the time president of the Assembly of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did the Assembly of Kosovo and, if you know, the Assembly of Vojvodina meet to give this approval?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: For Vojvodina it was the 10th of March, and for Kosovo it was the 23rd of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I thought Vojvodina's Assembly met on the 21st of March, but what you say is true. The session of the Assembly of Kosovo over which you presided took place on the 23rd of March. Tell me, was it a public session?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The session of the Kosovo parliament was a public one. It was attended by a great number of journalists. Never in my life, although I occupied various posts, had I spoken before a greater number of the press. There were 180 journalists accredited from all over Yugoslavia and even from abroad. The interest was huge in the course and the work of that particular session of the Assembly of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Jokanovic, was this parliament session held in a regular way?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: This parliament session was held quite regularly, in keeping with the constitution of Kosovo and in keeping with the Rules of Procedure of that parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were the speaker of that parliament. What was the ethnicity of other high officials in the parliament?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I was president, the vice-president was Albanian, general secretary was also Albanian. Since the parliament had three Chambers, in two Chambers there were Albanians, and in the third one there was a Montenegrin at the top. And my in my previous posts I also had a lot of Albanian colleagues. I think I explained that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, was any pressure exerted on the delegates?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: To vote or not to vote?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they pressured into accepting the proposal to consent to these constitutional amendments?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: We functioned in the system of delegates. Delegates voted in accordance with their constituency. Their constituency were the municipal assemblies, and the delegates of social political Chambers and various political organisations. Pressures in the sense of threats or any other kinds of pressure did not exist. It was the duty of the delegates to vote in accordance with the position of those organs who sent them to the Assembly of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Actually to vote in accordance with the position of their constituency?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, on the 3rd of May, 2002, Ibrahim Rugova stated here, I'm quoting his words, I took this off the transcript: "The Kosovo Assembly had to decide on the suspension of the status of Kosovo from the federation and the Assembly delegates were pressured into voting on this. The public was against this. They used violence to pressure them. There were tanks in the streets, and there were secret agents inside the Assembly building so that the members voted under pressure. I remember that ten members voted against, and these members were punished, convicted. Some were sent to prison, and some were fired." All right. So you were the president of the Assembly. Let us clear up some things. Were there any tanks around the Assembly building?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, there were no tanks around the Assembly building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any tanks? How did you come to the Assembly building from your house? Did you walk there or did you come with an escort or something like that?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the distance is relatively short. I lived in what was then called Beogradska Street. I went there on foot. I saw no tanks on the streets, no tanks around the Assembly building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, please have in mind the warning of the interpreters. As both of us speak Serbian, we have to make a pause in order to allow the interpreters to interpret what both of us say. So there was no pressure, and there were no tanks. But the fact that ten members of the Assembly voted against is an accurate one that can be confirmed by the minutes?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many members of the Kosovo Assembly attended that session where amendments were passed?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Hundred and 87.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the total number?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Hundred and ninety.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So only three members of the then-Kosovo Assembly did not attend the session?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And out of those 187, Rugova himself stated that ten voted against, and how many refrained from voting?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Ten voted against, and two delegates abstained from voting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So everybody else voted for?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody else voted for. This was a vast majority, and the decision was followed by an applause. Everybody stood up, because in addition to working nature, this was also a formal, solemn Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, did anybody from Serbia have an influence over the election of the members of the Kosovo Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The Republic of Serbia and its organs had no influence over the personnel policy in Kosovo. The personnel policy in Kosovo was something that was dealt with by Kosovo organs and other institutions in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there are documents to confirm all of these facts that you are testifying about. There were 187 delegates attending out of a total number of 190, ten voted against, 2 abstained from voting. How would you characterise the claim contained in paragraph 86 of this so-called indictment which reads as follows, I'm quoting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm stopping you. The indictment is proper as to form and to substance. Challenges were made at a preliminary stage, and they were dealt with. The indictment is a reality. It is entirely proper and should not be referred to in that way. Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, the indictment is an act of insolence, because everything in it is turned upside down. Not a single count --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have cut you off. If you are going to proceed in that manner concerning issues that have already been dealt with, I will not allow you to do so. I want to hear nothing more about the indictment. That issue has been dealt with, was dealt with from over two years ago. Proceed with your questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Well, here is an example of how it has been dealt with, Mr. Robinson. You don't need a greater example from this testimony of this witness. So paragraph 86 reads as follows: "The Kosovo Assembly met in March in Kosovo, and they voted on the proposed amendments," which is correct again. And I will quote on: "And most of the Kosovo Albanian delegates abstained from voting," which is a blatant lie, because only two of them abstained from voting. And then I continue quoting: "Although lacking the required two-thirds majority in the Assembly --" which again is a blatant lie, because only ten delegates voted against --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there will come a time when you will be allowed to make a speech. That time is not now. The evidence is to be elicited through the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Check the paragraph number again. I couldn't follow. You said 86.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said 86. 86, yes. Then it goes on to say: "Although the majority of Kosovo Albanian delegates abstained from voting. Although lacking the required two-thirds majority in the Assembly, the president of the Assembly nonetheless declared that the amendments --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that Mr. Milosevic is reading out of paragraph 81.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Anoya. Perhaps I had an old version, but the text is identical, and the new number is paragraph 81. I have it in English, and what I quoted is accurate, even in this new paragraph number. And it says here: "On 23rd March, [In English] Assembly of Kosovo met in Pristina and with the majority of Kosovo Albanian delegates abstaining, voted to accept the proposed amendments to the constitution. Although lacking the required two-thirds majority in the Assembly, the president of the Assembly nonetheless declared that amendments had passed." [Interpretation] And then in the end there's another sentence. It is not important for this witness: "[In English] Assembly of Serbia voted to approve the constitutional change, effectively revoking the autonomy granted in the 1974 constitution." [Interpretation] This is precisely what I read out verbatim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, out of 187 delegates, two voted against -- two abstained, ten voted against, and 174 voted for; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All of these delegates who had some reservations and who voted against, were they given an opportunity to speak publicly in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The session was held in a democratic atmosphere. All of those who wanted the floor were granted the right to speak, and you can see that in the tape recording. All of those who wanted were able to discuss publicly. I think that a lot of those who voted for also spoke up publicly. I think that there were a total of 34 people taking the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I think 34. I have it here in a press excerpt, because the press, on the following day, wrote about all of these facts that I'm describing here. It wrote about the debate, about those who attended, and so on. And there is also a videotape which is not complete because our technical facilities were not very modern at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the ethnic distribution of the membership of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ethnic composition was in accordance with the ethnic composition of the population. Therefore, there were over 70 per cent of Albanian delegates in the Assembly, and at the time there were 77 per cent of Albanians living in Kosovo and Metohija, and in the Assembly over 70 per cent of the delegates were Albanian. If I remember well, there were 140 and something -- 142 or 143 Albanian delegates in the Assembly. And then we had Serbs, Montenegrins, Turks, Muslims, and so on, again in numbers corresponding the ethnic composition of the population, because we had to satisfy the requirement for representation both as far as the ethnic composition was concerned and the social composition. That was very important in our then-system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Jokanovic. I have here the English translation and the Serbian text, so there are no problems with translations here. I also have the tape recording from the session of the Assembly held on the 23rd of March, 1989. I marked certain portions. You received this text in English. This is Exhibit 963. And I ask that this be admitted into evidence. You will be surprised to hear that even those who voted against did not have very firm views, were not firmly opposed to the constitutional amendments. However, it is their democratic right to vote, so there is no problem there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow the number you said 963 is coming from.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the number indicated on the list. It says here "DPK 963, tape recording," and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 65 ter number, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, my question was, Mr. Jokanovic -- in view of the significance, I have to repeat this question. In view of these facts that you are testifying about, and in view of these documents, how can you qualify the claims in paragraph 81 - and I thank Mr. Kwon for helping me with this - this claim that on the 23rd of March, 1989 the Assembly of Kosovo met in Pristina and, with the majority of Kosovo Albanian delegates abstaining, voted to accept the proposed amendments even though the required two-thirds majority was lacking, and the president of the Assembly - meaning you - declared that the amendments had passed, full stop. On the 28th of March, 1989 the Assembly of Serbia voted to approve the constitutional changes effectively revoking the autonomy granted in the 1974 constitution. So this is paragraph 81 of the English version. So please tell me, in view of these facts that you told us here, how do you assess this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: This is not correct. This is fabricated. This fabrication is an attempt to justify what was going on in Kosovo. I think that the Office of the Prosecution received this information which they deemed to be reliable. They received this -- these facts from those who use such fabrications to strengthen their separatist objectives of breaking Kosovo away from Serbia and transforming it into an independent state. I don't think that something like this, a claim like this, is even logical. I don't think that it would even be possible, realistic, because as a speaker of the parliament, I'm not a magician, so I could not, in the presence of 187 delegates, and in the presence of 180 journalists, in a situation where all leaders, the most prominent leaders from Kosovo and from the federation were present, how could I, under those circumstances, say the amendments have been passed when, in fact, they have not? The press reporting both in Serbian and Albanian will clearly show that the situation was, as will the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we play the tape, Mr. Robinson? And this will allow you to gain an impression. We have a videotape, a very brief one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please play the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Stop the tape. Mr. Milosevic, was it your intention to have the tape played without there being any translation? Because we're not getting any translation, so it's -- it's of no use to us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not my intention to play it without interpretation, because I assumed that it could be translated because it's very brief when you play the tape. So I thought that what is being spoken and what is being seen about all the organs supporting the Assembly session, that there was major interest in that, I thought that several of these key things could be interpreted. But we can continue. You can see what the atmosphere at the Assembly session itself was like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, before we continue, let me find out whether the interpreters are in a position to translate, to interpret.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's very fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I just heard that. The interpreters say the speech is very, very fast. It's very difficult for them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Without a transcript, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The following clip is not very fast, and it's pretty indicative, and I think it will show the actual place where the Assembly was held and the declaration of the adoption of the amendments. We do not have to interpret this very fast clip, but let's look at the next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if you could also indicate the relevant page number of this transcript. It's not interpreted?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This next clip, you will see now and then I will try with the help of the witness to identify when it was taken and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "There is the Socialist Republic of Serbia became a state throughout its territory after the decision of the republican -- after the parliament on Kosovo the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Serbia will be announced on the 28th of March. It is well known that the provincial parliament of Kosovo gave its approval to the wording of the amendments."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Jokanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you proceed, let me ask the witness, just to clarify this. There's a reference to paragraph 81 of the indictment to which Mr. Milosevic referred. You say it is -- it does not reflect the factual situation because the reference to the required two-thirds majority not being present is wrong because there was a two-thirds majority. Please answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a two-thirds majority and agreement was reached by an overwhelming majority, much greater than a two-thirds majority. A two-thirds majority was required, however, under the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that in declaring the amendments as having passed, you acted entirely properly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I acted completely properly, in accordance with my agenda and in the way I conducted the meeting, asked who was for, who was against, how many abstained, and I declared that agreement was reached on the amendments to the constitution of Serbia, and this was followed, as you could see, by applause. All the deputies who were present got to their feet. This happened before 180 journalists and TV crews who happened to be accredited for that event that day. I have the original newspapers with me where what I'm saying now was published at the time. These are both newspapers in Serbian. I also have a newspaper in the Albanian language, Jedinstvo Politika in Albanian. It's the newspaper Rilindja Komunist. There are pictures and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You've answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, at the moment when you declared the amendments adopted and when the Assembly session got to its feet and the applause began, we could see on this brief clip many figures who were sitting there. Can you please remember and tell us who we can see. Who was sitting in the front row? Who were those who were present as special guests and who also applauded and got to their feet and so on?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The session was attended by leaders and officials from the federation who were representing Kosovo in the federation. The member of the Presidency of Yugoslavia was there. The member of the Presidency of the Central Committee of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you, Mr. Jokanovic, but it would be useful, if you remember, if you could also tell us their names and not only just their posts.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Member of the Presidency of Yugoslavia who was before the vice-president and the president of the Presidency, his name is Sinan Hasani.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: He's an Albanian from the village of Pozharanje from my own municipality Kosovska Vitina. He's also a writer, an author, who published the first novel in the Albanian language. He's a very prominent, respected figure. He's a novelist called "Rrushi ka filluar me u pjek." That's in Albanian. In Serbian the title is The Grapes are Beginning to Ripen. Next to him was Ali Shukrija, who was a member of the Presidency of the Central Committee of Yugoslavia. Remzi Koleci, the president of the Presidency of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Remzi Shukrija [sic] Was also an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, an Albanian from Kosovska Mitrovica. He participated in World War II and was decorated for that, and he was in the political life of Kosovo and the federation for many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Continue. Remzi Koleci, what about him?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Remzi Koleci was the president of the Presidency of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo. This is the top function in Kosovo. Rrahman Morina, the president of the Presidency of the Provincial Committee of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All Albanians?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Albanian. Daut Jasanica, the president of the Presidency of the Socialist Alliance of the Albanians. The president of the Executive Council, also an Albanian, Nazmi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that Jusuf Zejnullahu who was the person at the time?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Jusuf Zejnullahu at the time actually -- actually, at the time it was either Nazmi Mustafa or Jusuf Zejnullahu. There are many years that have gone by since then and there were people always changing in those functions. I think it was Jusuf Zejnullahu.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure either. I'm trying to remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Jokanovic, at the last page of this transcript I notice you were saying at the time, "Those in favour, please raise your hands. And who is against?" My question is whether this method of voting, which is raising their hands, is a usual method of voting at the Assembly, instead of using some ballot paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the usual method of voting, not only in Kosovo but also in the republic and in the other republics. Voting was public, by acclamation, by the raising of one's hand. It was also possible to have a secret ballot if a delegate proposed such a measure and the Assembly agreed to have a secret vote. In this case, there were no such proposals. It's possible that nobody proposed such a measure because all the organs in the province and all the municipal assemblies in the province had already made their decisions and obliged their delegates to vote in accordance with their constituency, which delegated them to come and vote. The reporter - and this was the clip that was not interpreted - says that the decision is based on the decision of all the forms of organs who coordinated and made the decision to vote in favour of the amendments. So the voting was public, and that was the practice. There was no electronic voting at the time. We did not have such a possibility then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, I have a very short question for you. It was you we saw on the video clip, was it, making the announcement? Who was the person who made the announcement immediately before we saw the applause?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was me. I was the president of the Kosovo Assembly, and that is my voice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm much younger, but that was me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. Now, the transcript we have ends with a reference to, "The Chambers of the Kosovo Assembly have agreed to hold a joint session of all three Chambers. We should now decide when shall we take a 20-minute break." Is the part that's on the video after the 20-minute break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, I would just like to explain something. This is the part that pertains to the constitution. Then the rest of the meeting deals with current issues and has nothing to do with this. What you have here only deals with the constitution. The session then proceeded to deal with regular matters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer, since the question was addressed to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Assembly began its work by sitting in the different -- in its separate Chambers. It set the agenda. The amendments were just the first item on the agenda. Then the other items were also adopted. When the session pertaining to the amendments was finished, the session went on to deal with the rest of the items on the agenda. But I was not presiding over that whole session. It was presided over by the presidents of the Chambers. The constitution continued its session. The opening speech was heard, which was submitted by the vice-president of the Executive Council, Kazeb Susuri [phoen], dealing with other matters, economic issues and other topics that were on the agenda. So the Assembly session continued with its regular work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps it's Mr. Milosevic who can answer the question, then. Where in the transcript do we find the part which we saw in the video?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on the last page in the Serbian version. It says when it was noted that there were ten against, that there were two abstentions, then it states: "I hereby declare that the Assembly of the Socialist Autonomous Province of Kosovo has approved the text of the amendments after democratic discussion, and this outcome of our Assembly session, allow me to say a few things." Then Mr. Jokanovic gives a brief speech, but then what you saw on the video was him declaring the Assembly approving the text of the amendments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it may be my mistake, but it's not how I saw it on the transcript but I'll review it later and clarify the position for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move on and while we're considering to the degree we are the transcript, and just in case the Chamber takes it with it when it adjourns very soon, there's a bit of a problem in handling this exhibit. It's most easily seen from the Serbian original but you can actually pick up the problem in the English transcript. As I hold up the Serbian original, which has page numbers in the top right-hand corner, you will see that pages are sequential to a degree until page 87, although there are missing pages. There's then a series of pages starting again at 24 and running through, in the original Serbian, to 88 by simply being a collection of pages which should probably be inserted into the earlier series of pages. But even, I think, by inserting them we don't have a complete record. If you look at the English version, you can see the problem at various places. For example, if you take the English version and look at page, bottom right-hand corner, 36, and then look to the top of that, you'll see that there is a reference there to the first three lines ending page 71 and the record picking up at page 74, indicating that pages 72 and 73 are missing. Now, I think you'll then find, if you go back to the collection of pages at the end, that 72 and 73 aren't here at all. So that we've got a slightly muddled record and, I think, an incomplete one. The accused may not have focused his attention on this. It may be something he will want to do during the forthcoming break in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you heard that. Some pages seem to be missing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I did hear what is being discussed. Sometimes it happens that the stenograms repeat several times, that they start from 1 and then some parts begin again, depending on the person who is actually transcribing the stenogram. You have page 7, then you have 10, then 35, then 37, and so on in the stenogram. As Mr. Nice rightly said, you have page 80, then 87 on the last pages in Serbian, but before that, for example, you have many pages. Before that you have 84, 85, 83, again 84, 82, 81, because this last page, 80, has the words Kurtesh Salihu, then Kurtesh Salihu, then a blank space. Many pages before that you have Kurtesh Salihu on page 81, then he says, "Comrades, delegates ..." and then you have his speech. So that means his speech was not dropped, it's just a question of how it was arranged. Mr. Jokanovic has already pointed out that the technical facilities were not the best for transcription. This is what we have. This is the actual stenogram that exists. There's also the video recording, which is also quite clear. There are the facts. I would just like to ask you, after the break, of course, because I know it's time for the break, that regardless of the fact that we did not translate this, because it's very difficult to translate the newspapers, you can admit not my photocopies, but you can admit the originals which Mr. Jokanovic has, where you can see in the newspapers from that time - for example, we will put that on the ELMO - we have a clip from Rilindja, which is the Albania newspaper, and you can see the entire Assembly session delegates on its feet. There is also the part by Sinan Hasani, the president of Yugoslavia. I can recognise him in the photo. I can recognise Ali Shukrija, I can recognise Rrahman Morina; all of these people that Mr. Jokanovic mentioned. So both in the transcripts and in the newspapers -- in the video clip and in the newspaper you can see all of these officials very well. So it -- there can be no doubt about the public nature of the meeting, the people who were present, the reporting from it. And you will not find anywhere in Albanian newspapers either any mention of any presence of police forces or any other nonsense that we heard in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Jokanovic, you will be pleased to know we're going to follow your practice by taking a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we considered in the break how to deal with these newspaper clips which you would like the witness to refer to and which are in his possession, not in yours. We have the same problem of translation, but if the passages are short, then they can be put on the ELMO and the interpreters can translate them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, there is no particular need to quote from the newspaper. I just wanted you to see them on the ELMO for you to see newspapers in Serbian, newspapers in Albanian, all the media coverage that accompanied this event which reflects the atmosphere of complete consensus that was typical, that characterised the enactment of the amendments. I have copies of the newspaper that Mr. Jokanovic has before him, and of course we have a full set of these newspapers, but they have not been translated. We thought it would be a waste of resources to make these translations. Everything is explained in both Albanian and in Serbian newspapers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but if -- if they're put on the ELMO, they'll have to be translated, and for that purpose we just want to have a specific portion or whatever it is identified so that it can be translated. Otherwise, it's not of any benefit to us. Alternatively, you could leave them, identify what you want to have translated, and we would have them submitted for translation, and we would mark them for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. That can be done on a general basis. I would just like to put a few things on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For instance, Mr. Jokanovic, would you please put on the ELMO the first -- the cover page of the Politika of the day following the passage of the amendments, 28th -- sorry, 24th of March, showing your picture. Show, please, this part where the text begins and where it says: "Twenty-four delegates took part in the discussion, in the debate. The amendments were passed by an overwhelming majority of votes (out of 187 delegates, ten were against, and two abstained.)" Then you see the highlighted part, and as Mr. Jokanovic explained, it also states the number of press representatives present, the number of deputies who took part in the debate, and the number of those who voted and how they voted. That's the front page of Politika. And now for the sake of balance, let us see the Rilindja newspaper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness confirm, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kept this copy of the newspaper in my own documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness. Witness. I just wanted to confirm whether what Mr. Milosevic read is in the paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the interpreters who should have translated it. What's the next newspaper, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will skip many newspapers in Serbian. Let us have the Albanian newspaper Rilindja. It is in this set.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And since you, Mr. Jokanovic, are fluent in Albanian, can you please interpret the headlines or, rather, the captions below the pictures. Do you see this on the ELMO? Because I don't have this copy before me. Let me just see if what you put on the ELMO is exactly what I meant. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why don't you -- is it the highlighted portions that he is to read?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He can read whatever he wants out of the highlights, but I would like him to read -- or, rather, to identify the people in the first row. This is an Albanian newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can see everybody standing and clapping. What is written below this photo, and who are people in the first row?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: It says in Albanian, because I know the Albanian language: "Deputies to the Kosovo parliament applauding the passage of amendments to the constitution of the Republic of Serbia." In the first row I'm showing Ali Shukrija, Rrahman Morina, both Albanians; Sinan Hasani, member of the Presidency of the SFRY, also Albanian; and Mr. Koleci, president of the Presidency of Kosovo, also Albanian. The headline is: "Approval given to amend the constitution of Serbia." Here, where I'm pointing, it says: "180 journalists and photo reporters." In another photograph you see the moment of voting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jokanovic. I will not go through any more of these newspapers, although there are many of them, including interviews with Albanian officials, their photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please play the third clip we have on the video recording showing the session of the Republic of Serbia parliament. I have been told that this is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have seen this. Next excerpt, please. This clip we have already seen. I was expecting the following clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When the clip is played, the interpreters should interpret if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This is fast, and the interpreters do not have the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I appreciate that, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Pursuant to Article 431 of the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Serbia and the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Serbia at the session of Chambers of associated labour, Chamber of municipalities, and the socio-political Chamber of the 28th of March, 1989, adopts the decision to proclaim amendments 9 to 49 to the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Serbia. Hereby proclaimed are amendments 9 to 49 to the constitution of the Republic of Serbia, as adopted by the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia at the sessions of the Chambers of associated labour, the Chamber of municipalities, and the socio-political Chamber, and as agreed by the assemblies of provinces, including the province of Vojvodina at the joint session of all Chambers held on the 10th of March and the provincial parliament of Kosovo at the joint session of all Chambers held on the 23rd of March, 1989."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Jokanovic. You had occasion to be reminded of this event by this video. You saw yourself in the first row. Who else did you recognise in the first row among the officials that you think are noteworthy?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I could see you. I could see Sinan Hasani. I could see the president of the federal government or, rather, the Prime Minister, Ante Markovic, as well as other prominent figures of our public life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Please tell me, Mr. Jokanovic, after the parliament session of the 23rd of March, did anyone, either in newspapers or in public speeches or maybe in a non-public way, at any gathering at all, question the procedure and the adoption of decisions in Kosovo regarding these amendments?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: There were no such objections voiced. On the contrary, and we can see that in the documents of the League of Communists of Kosovo, it was considered a great victory of the progressive forces in Kosovo. It was considered to be a great victory of progressive forces over the separatists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But were there any objections at that session of the parliament of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear any such objections, at least not before 1987 when a journalist from Kosovo, who I believe testified here, asked me about the course of that session and told me approximately something to the effect of the words in this indictment, and I answered him the same way as I testified under oath before this honourable Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the parliament session of the 23rd of March, you had talks with the delegation of the European parliament that visited Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A very high-placed delegation of the European parliament arrived. I received them and acquainted them with the general situation and with the progress made in Kosovo. I spoke to them about the constitutional amendments and the problems we are facing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We have to save time. Did they have any objections or observations? Did they question in any way the procedure in the course of that parliamentary session? Did they voice any problems they might have had about the amendments?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They had no objections, they had no questions as to the course of the session. That was not in dispute at all. After that, I held a press conference for all the domestic and foreign journalists, and I answered a great series of questions, and none of the accredited journalists had any questions or doubts as to the work of the parliamentary session. The same is true of the European parliamentarians and all the future meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After the passage of the amendments, and I don't mean several minutes later when the session continued after the 20-minute break, I mean in the following weeks and months, did the parliament of Kosovo continue to operate normally?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: It operated normally, and already in May I was re-elected speaker or president of the parliament of Kosovo for another one-year term.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was in May, because your term of office of one year had expired.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And that was two months after this session.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was re-elected unanimously. At that same session, the member of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, Riza Sapundzija was re-elected by secret ballot. Two candidates were nominated for the Presidency of Kosovo. One of these candidates is not receive the necessary number of votes and was not elected into the Presidency. The Assembly continued to work normally and in June it adopted amendments to the constitution of Kosovo. These amendments to the Kosovo constitution harmonised the Kosovo constitution with the constitution of the Republic of Serbia and the amendments that had previously been adopted by the Federal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What about this June session of the Kosovo parliament? Did it have any problems, and how did it work?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: It worked quite normally. Again, as usual, I held an introductory speech. I have reports to corroborate it here. The amendments were again passed unanimously by the same Assembly, the same deputies, just as happened at the previous session of the 23rd of March which only gave approval to the amendments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, now, what happened, if you know, because after the expiry of your second term of office a new speaker of the parliament was elected, so if you know, tell us how the parliament continued to work in 1990. As far as I understand, until the end of your term of office, there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I thanked the deputies. I still have the speech that I held then. And after that, elections were held for the new parliament of Kosovo. The parliament of Kosovo was elected in a new composition. Sixty-four per cent of the citizens voted, and that parliament worked normally at the beginning, electing Djordje Bozovic as president. From December to June it worked normally. In June, very serious problems occurred in the work of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that because at the time I was vice-president of the Serbian Assembly, and the president of the Assembly, Djordje Bozovic, talked to the president of the Serbian Assembly who then informed me, in view of the fact that I am from Kosovo, telling us that there were problems in the Assembly because a group of deputies wanted, outside of the agenda and beyond of the rules of procedure, to declare a declaration on independence of Kosovo and the fact that Kosovo was a republic. So this was the position taken by one group of deputies. The other group of deputies opposed that. The normal working procedure was disrupted, and the president of the Assembly, Djordje Bozovic, had to -- had to disrupt the session on a number of occasions because there was a danger that clashes would erupt between the deputies. One set of deputies wanted to follow the agenda and the established procedure, whereas another set of deputies wanted to read out the declaration on the independence of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, who was in that group who wanted to read the declaration on the independence of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I was not there, I was not present. The official statements always identified them as a group of deputies who apparently read out this declaration in front of the Assembly building, in front of the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you don't know how many people were in that group?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not in Kosovo at the time. I can give you secondhand information from the then president of the Kosovo Assembly who said that there were about 40 deputies in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. He said about 40 of them. And the total number of deputies was the same as when you were the president, 190?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 190 because the constitution was the same and I don't know exactly how many people were in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the cause for that reaction of those deputies?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the cause was the situation in Yugoslavia. Yugoslavia started disintegrating already. Slovenia and Croatia had already declared their independence, and a group of these deputies in Kosovo thought it was the right moment for them to take the same path and to declare Kosovo an independent republic. They naturally picked a moment that was most advantageous for their causes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this attempt of theirs to read the declaration on the steps outside the Assembly building took place after the event that you mentioned, the declaration of independence of Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So after they had announced their intention to secede.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the intention of Slovenia to break away from Yugoslavia was clear. The situation was already such that federal organs were not functioning properly. Neither was the League of Communists. So the situation was very tense, and that kind of atmosphere was very beneficial to those who had the design of turning Kosovo into an independent republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So Djordje Bozovic, who was your successor in that post, who was the president of the Assembly after that, what did he do? He went and spoke to the president of the Serbian Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They had telephone contacts and other contacts. And then one day the president of the Assembly, with a large group of deputies, came to Belgrade. He demanded a meeting. He wanted a solution to be found, because he believed that that wasn't his responsibility alone; that was something that the republican organs had to deal with. And then a large meeting was organised, attended by the top leaders from Serbia, including a group of deputies from Kosovo. During that meeting, Djordje Bozovic briefed everyone on the problems. He said that the situation was abnormal, and he could not continue with his regular work, and as president of the Assembly, he could not allow the Kosovo to be declared a republic, and he did not want to be held responsible for that. He wanted instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was my position regarding that?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I attended that meeting together with the president of the Assembly who took me along in view of the fact that I was from Kosovo. Other leaders from Serbia also attended the meeting, not just leaders from Assembly but also from other organs, and I can give you their names because I remember those people. Milo Nirminic [phoen], was there, Zoran Andjelkovic, and so on. However, the deputies from Kosovo were persistent, including Djordje Bozovic. They wanted the Assembly to be dissolved temporarily. That was a key issue. And then Djordje Bozovic also wanted to inform the president of the Presidency - I believe you held that post at the time, I think you did - so you came and attended that meeting briefly. You were informed on what was going on, and your position was that they ought to go back to Pristina and use the rules of procedure, apply them to give the floor to those who wanted to speak, and those who were against the declaration had to use that procedure to speak, although you spoke very decisively, very firmly. Djordje Bozovic was somewhat anxious, and he stood up, and those others from Serbia who attended the meeting, they said, after your arrival, "Well, Djordje, perhaps you could still continue with the work." And Djordje said, "No. I'm not the president of the Assembly any more," and you left the meeting, saying that the Assembly should go on with its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, the Assembly could not continue with its work.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not under normal, regular circumstances. Djordje Bozovic was still president of the Assembly, and the deputies officially demanded a temporary dissolution of the Assembly of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the session of the Assembly actually commenced.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: It was scheduled, and it actually commenced, and the then deputy Stane Dolenc on behalf of the deputies who were against that move, condemned the conduct of the other group of deputies. He said that there was no other solution but to dissolve the Assembly. And then problems ensued, commotion, dissatisfaction of certain deputies, and then Djordje Bozovic again disrupted or brought the session to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were any decisions adopted?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No decisions were adopted. Simply a demand was addressed to the Assembly of Serbia to dissolve the Kosovo Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did the Serbian Assembly adopt this demand? Did it approve it?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't present, so I couldn't tell you what was the result of the vote. The atmosphere was not a regular one. However, this demand was read out, and then a commotion ensued. The deputies wanted this to be forwarded to the Serbian Assembly, and it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the reaction of the Serbian Assembly when it received this demand?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: In one of its sessions, which I did not attend for some private reasons, the Serbian Assembly in this session held in the afternoon hours adopted the law on temporary dissolution of the Assembly of Kosovo and the Executive Council of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you just stated about the position of the Assembly and the deputies of the Kosovo Assembly, and then you said that the Serbian Assembly adopted the decision to dissolve the Kosovo Assembly temporarily.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. What can you tell us about the so-called Kacanik constitution?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm very familiar with that term. It was frequently mentioned in the media. I went to that area frequently. Kacanik is a small town in Kosovo where an illegal session was held. Some deputies attended the session. I don't know exactly who attended it, but secondhand or thirdhand information indicate that the then vice-president of the Serbian Assembly chaired that session and the session was held there. Now, who exactly was present there and what exactly transpired there is something that nobody really knows. But at any rate, the press described that as an illegal gathering contrary to the Kosovo constitution, constitution of Serbia, constitution of Yugoslavia, and it was a mono-ethnic session. At the time, mono-ethnic decisions or decisions lacking the proper procedural requirements were considered invalid, especially if they were passed in violation of the constitution of Yugoslavia, constitution of Serbia, and constitution of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was in violation of all of these constitutions. All right. And finally, please tell me briefly, what were your personal relations with Albanians that you lived and worked with in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born, I grew up there. I was friends with Albanians. I played with them as a child. We went to each other's houses, went to school together. I have a lot of friends who are Albanian both when I was a child and later on. To this day, I continue my contacts with not an insignificant number of Albanians, mostly telephone contacts, but not with Albanians in the territory of Kosovo but, rather, in the territory of Central Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, what happened to your birth town, your birthplace, the village where you were born? What is the situation like there now?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the situation is tragic. Prior to the arrival of KFOR, my village had 35 houses inhabited by Serbs, ten households of Roma residents. All of these houses were first looted and then destroyed so that nowadays there is not a single Serbian or Roma house left intact, including my own, although Albanian neighbours wanted to protect my house and some other houses in the village; however, that put themselves under risk. As they told me, they were threatened that they could be liquidated. My friend, Albanian, sent me photographs of my house. So if you want me --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO. As I understood it, they first protected your houses, and then after that they were powerless to do anything else?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: After that, they were powerless. Not only my house. They wanted to protect the house of my relative Bane Petrovic, who had helped some people there, protected them from a paramilitary group, and they even gave guarantees to Bane Petrovic, telling him to remain there in the village. However, the guarantees lasted only some 15 days, and after that the same neighbours told him, "We cannot protect you any longer." So he moved out. And in the meantime, a friend of mine was also killed, Mr. Radenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Just put it on the ELMO, these photographs, and this will bring the examination to a conclusion. So this is your house in the village of Grmovo in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my house as it looked before and after the arrival of KFOR. This is my house. This is my house as it looked, and nowadays there is nothing left. Nothing remains of my house. The church has also been destroyed, and a lot of monuments desecrated as well. However, this was not done initially, at the very beginning. Initially, only three Serb houses were set on fire, the houses belonging to those who bore arms, in the police or in the army. And only after some 15 days, as Albanian neighbours told us, slowly they started taking off construction material, roof tiles, doors, windows, and so on, everything that could be detached, and then they continued destroying the houses, whereas the church was blown up by an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jokanovic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, where do you now live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the status in our terminology of a temporarily displaced person. Therefore, in reality, I'm a refugee, currently living in Belgrade. My two sons were in Pristina, however, they live in Belgrade now as well, as do my other relatives who are dispersed throughout Serbia, living in various collective shelters and various outbuildings, and all of them used to be quite wealthy people before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we are going to deal with the exhibits from the examination-in-chief now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. There's, of course, the issue of the transcript, which I understood the accused was going to take the witness to as to some extracts. We haven't returned to that at all, but that's a matter for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First we have to deal with the records of political meetings of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia and Kosovo. Should we give the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number is D253.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be marked for identification until the translation is done. And the next, tape recording of the joint session. Transcript, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be marked as D254.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And next we have two news clips, first from Politika and second from Rilindja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then video clips.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Video clips, D256.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And finally, the photos.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The photos will be marked as D257.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is there anything else you want to exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you like the ID admitted as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't know. Mr. Milosevic, do you want the ID, the identification, admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you believe it to be useful, useful evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's for you to determine, not for us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let it be admitted then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Okay. So the ID will be marked as D258.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, are you ready to hand over the photos as well as the ID? Or you can just hand over a photocopy of the ID.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if possible, I would like to hand over a photocopy. And if you believe it to be important, I'm ready to give up my ID and even these photographs which are important to me. They're a memento. Because once you lose your home place, then you've lost a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We can have copies made of them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, since the witness had some other documents pertaining to a large number of meetings on constitutional changes and from which you could see how broad this activity was, how free the discussions were, what was discussed, this is a whole set of documents. So if you believe that this would be of some use to you, I believe that they could be admitted as exhibits. I did not have time to deal with them in detail because I simply -- my time simply went by much faster than I expected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that's not the procedure. We can't just admit documents like that. You have to introduce them through the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a large number of them, and of course I was interested to know to which particular parts of them, if any, we were going in order that I could deal with them. As far as I'm concern, I obviously -- it's a matter for the Chamber and the accused how long he's allowed in evidence with any particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we won't admit those. Mr. Nice, you may begin your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. For my part, if it were convenient for the Chamber, I would prefer to start tomorrow because I was expecting to deal with a large number of additional documents and the documents we would wish to put to the witness have yet to be marshalled and prepared in an easily usable way. If you wish me to start today, of course I can and I can put a couple of documents on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. I think you may start, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As you please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard a lot about publicity from you, in local press, and we've heard a lot about allegations of bias in Western press. So I'm afraid we don't have this copied in the way I would most prefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May this document go on the overhead projector, please. Thank you very much. First page. We're going to go through it all. And Your Honour, what I would suggest is, if you allow me this indulgence, we'll just look at this document today and then I'll produce it tomorrow in such form as is convenient for all of these exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic what we have here, and I'll read from my version, is something from the Washington Post of November the 29th, 1986. And it includes within it --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
