utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it Mr. Nice's obligation, if he wishes to submit a document, to also provide a copy for me and not only provide a copy for the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you gave an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think he's going to produce that tomorrow. In the circumstances, we can proceed. You can see it on the -- on your monitor, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jokanovic, this report, as we're going to discover, includes the product of an interview with yourself, but I'd like you, please, to help us with the general picture painted here for November of 1986.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Will Your Honours give me one minute. In order that things can be done sequentially, I'd rather start with the one of 1982. It's the same topic, that is, how Kosovo's problems were being described externally. You can put mine on and I'll read it on the screen. Thank you. I'll read, I hope, slowly enough. It comes from Pristina. Can you just show me the top of the document so that we can see the headline and byline. No, right at the top first. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: New York Times, July the 12th, 1982. "Exodus of Serbians stirs province in Yugoslavia" by Marvine Howe. Dateline Pristina. "Danilo Krstic and his family are hardworking wheat and tobacco farmers, Serbs who get along with their Albanian neighbours. "'You have to love the place where you live to stay on the land here,' Marko Krstic, the eldest son, told visitors to the farm at Bec, a few miles from the Albanian border. There have been no serious troubles between Serbians and Albanians in Bec, but Serbs in some of the neighbouring villages have reportedly been harassed by Albanians and have packed up and left the region. "The exodus of Serbs is admittedly one of the main problems that the authorities have to content with in Kosovo, an autonomous province of Yugoslavia, inhabited largely by Albanians. "Rioting Brought Awareness. "Last year's riots --" so that would be the 1981 riots, Mr. Jokanovic -- "in which nine people were killed, shocked not only the troubled province of Kosovo but also the entire country into an awareness of the problems of this most backward part of Yugoslavia, which is made up of many ethnic groups. "In June a 43-year-old Serb, Miodrag Saric, was shot and killed by an Albanian neighbour, Ded Krasniqi, in a village near Djakovica, 40 miles south-west of Pristina. According to the official Yugoslavia press agency TANJUG, it was the second murder of a Serb by an Albanian in Kosovo this year. The dispute reportedly started with a quarrel over damage done to a field belonging to the Saric family. "The local political and security bodies condemned the murder as 'a grave criminal act' that could have serious repercussions, according to the press agency. Five members of the Krasniqi family have been arrested and investigations are continuing. "The authorities have responded at various levels to violence in Kosovo, clearly trying to avoid antagonising the Albanian majority. Besides firm security measures, action has been taken to speed political, educational, and economic changes." There's then a short headline, "Past Errors Acknowledged." "Privately, some officials acknowledge that the rise of Albanian nationalism in a society that is based on the principle of equality of nationalities is the result of past errors - at first neglect and discrimination, and more recently failure to act against divisive forces or even to recognise them." I'll pause there. We're going to look at the rest of this article which includes your own contributions to it, but there is a suggestion here of recognition of past errors, neglect and discrimination against Albanians. Do you accept that this is a fair description of the position at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is not proper, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because neglect and discrimination is not being spoken about vis-a-vis the Albanians but vis-a-vis the Serbs. This is something that is being ignored.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is not for the accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the question is quite legitimate and proper. The witness is to answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, if you could just repeat your question briefly so that I'm sure to understand it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. Of the last paragraph I've read to you, where it describes an acknowledgement by officials at the rise of Albanian nationalism was based -- arose in part as a result of past errors, at first neglect and discrimination - I'll come to the last bit later - do you accept that neglect and discrimination, and I'll be neutral, discrimination against one group or another, was a cause of the rise of nationalism?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: This article and what you are asking me now refers to mistakes in the past by Albanians committed against Serbs. So this is the spirit of the article. Mistakes from the past are discussed here, because in the past Albanian nationalism was not dealt with, which made it possible for it to spread. In 1981, this was the assessment of official organs of the province and the federation, and they drew the consequences, and those who were in power were punished in the province because of discrimination and the exodus of Serbs. I think that these are the mistakes that are being talked about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. It goes on, if you remember this paragraph, to say: "More recently, a failure to act against divisive forces or even to recognise them." Now, "forces" are in the plural, "divisive" is the description. What do you say? Just one divisive force or were there more than one?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The demonstrations themselves in 1981, as I have already said, considerably disrupted inter-ethnic relations, and there was a cooling in relations between neighbours, between the different groups. Albanian nationalists, whose objective was an ethnically pure Kosovo, felt that it was favourable for them to disrupt these relations and to cause conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So again, it's all the Albanians' fault, is it? I just want to be quite sure what your position is and whether you think this newspaper's got it right.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: As I understand it, this article adopts a realistic approach towards the position of Serbs, the killing of Serbs, and the errors committed by the Kosovo leadership as well as the causes which led to these large demonstrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The killing of Serbs by 1982, the time of this article, yes? You're saying that that was already well under way, was it?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I said in my testimony that there were already killings. There were also other forms of pressure. And I cited in my testimony these very same examples that are given in the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Read on a little, then. "The nationalists have a two-point platform, according to Becir Hoti, an executive secretary of the Communist Party of Kosovo, first to establish what they call an ethnically clean Albanian republic, and then the merger with Albania to form a Greater Albania. "Mr. Hoti, an Albanian, expressed concern over political pressures that were forcing Serbs to leave Kosovo. What is important now, he said, is to establish a climate of security and create confidence." Next page, please. Thank you very much. If we can go to the top of the page. Or if the -- thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I should say this should be the last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "The migration of Serbs is no ordinary problem, because Kosovo is the heartland of Serbian history, culture, and religion. Serbs have been in this region since the seventh century, long before they founded their own independent dynasty." And then this: "Fifty-seven thousand have left the region. Some 57.000 Serbs have left Kosovo in the last decade and the number increased considerably after the riots of March and April last year, according to Vukasin Jokanovic, another executive secretary of the Kosovo party." Well, that's you, isn't it, Mr. Jokanovic?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your evidence -- not your evidence, your contribution on this topic to the newspaper at this stage was that the riots of the previous year, which you say were all Albanian separatist inspired, drove some 57 -- no, not 57.000 Serbs but drove a number of Serbs out of the community; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: That's probably what I said. The number of those who moved out is probably much greater over a longer period, but this is probably the figure that I gave at the time. I cannot remember this interview. Becir Hoti, by the way, is a person that I know, and what he is describing was the actual state of affairs at the time, just as it was what I was saying. He was an Albanian, I was a Serb, we were implementing the same policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, Your Honour, we'll come back to this tomorrow. If I can have that version back, then we will provide this and the other open-source material that we'll be relying on in part in a compendious form that will be easy to handle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, we're going to adjourn now. We're going to adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 2nd day of December, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
